chunks: Which chips are PoP and why. The question: Which chips are often PoP? Why?
PoP is mostly used on the main processors of phones and tablets, with a low-power memory chip stacked on top. Some small boards, wearables and cameras use it too.
It suits chips that have little board space, use only a few watts, and are made in huge numbers. Big power-hungry chips such as server processors and graphics chips do not use it.
Bunk beds suit a small room: stacking saves floor space. The top bunk is warmer, because heat rises. In a big house with lots of floor, people put the beds side by side.
A phone is the small room. A server is the big house, with needs of its own: far more memory, and a heat sink on its chip.
PoP passes three gates: area is critical, power is a few watts, and memory is fixed at assembly.
Phone, tablet and similar AP-class chips pass all three; servers, GPUs and desktop CPUs fail at least one.
Application processor: the main chip of a phone or tablet, which runs the operating system. SoC (system on chip): one chip holding the processor and many other blocks.
LPDDR: low-power memory used in phones. DIMM: a plug-in memory stick used in PCs and servers.
HBM: memory dies stacked and placed right beside a large processor, to move huge amounts of data per second.
Take a 14 mm times 14 mm processor, which is 196 mm², and a memory package of 11 mm times 11. 5 mm.
Side by side with 1 mm of gap and 1 mm of keep-out room on each side, they need about (14 + 11 + 2) times 14 = 378 mm² of board. Stacked, they need only the processor's 196 mm².
That saves about 48% of the area. A server processor is the opposite case.
It burns tens to hundreds of watts, needs a heat sink on its chip, and needs far more memory than a stacked package holds. So it uses DIMMs instead. That is the whole idea.
"PoP is mostly for mobile application processors, the SoCs in phones and tablets, with LPDDR stacked on top, and similar compact embedded SoCs.
They fit because they're area- and height-constrained, use LPDDR where a very short link saves power and timing, run at a few watts so the thermal penalty is manageable, and ship in huge volumes.
Servers, desktop CPUs, GPUs and FPGAs don't use it: too much power and heat, and they need DIMMs, GDDR or HBM for capacity and bandwidth."
